title: 'Every Time I Fall in Love', scat chorus and 'Loch Lomond'
summary: She describes an old song worked out with Wilber, a scat chorus, and the album's repertoire including 'As Long As I Live'.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And, of course, 'Every Time; Every Time I Fall In Love' -- I don't know where I heard that first -- but I had been doing that for a long time, too.
I like it. It's a good number. It has more like a little dixieland or a real jazz feeling. And when --
Bob Wilber had a hard time trying to listen. When he brought in the music, it was very old, and it began to sort of wear at the edges.
And it had --
Could you just say or speak or sing the first line of the -- the first two lines of the song? Because there's another song with a very similar title.
Yeah, I know what you mean. (Singing)
"Every time, every time, every doggone time I fall in love, I get a shoving around every time; Every time, every time, every doggone

time I try romance, I'm taking a chance on losing my mind; I'm gonna learn to be a hermit, live in a hermit's cage; Until I lose the blues my baby gave to me, I'm gonna burn my bridges behind me; I'm gonna hide out and then, you could look but you'll never find me; Behind the eight ball again 'cause; Every time, every time, every doggone time I fall in love, I get a shoving around every doggone time."
Wow, all right. That's more of a performance that I had expected.

I said it was real frayed at the edges and no wonder, I forget what year it was written in. But the cover had characters on there that were drawn by a female cartoonist -- Parker was her last name. And the characters were like Flapper Fanny. That goes back quite a bit. And it was written
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
by Gordon Jenkins.
Oh.

Yeah. So that had to be in the 20's -- I guess the late 20's, maybe 1930. But anyway, I liked it, I keep that in my repertoire. "Jeepers Creepers," I wanted to do because I hadn't recorded it. That was from Going Places -- the movie that I had the opportunity to do with Louie Armstrong.
Yeah.

Bob Wilber suggested that we do a -- I guess you would call it a scat version of "Rocking in Rhythm." It's not exactly a scat version, but I sing the part of one of the instruments of "Rockin' in Rhythm." And that was his idea. Not too bad.
Not at all.
Turned out pretty good. And, of course, "Loch Lomond"! I think
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Bill was a little afraid that I wouldn't be identified enough unless I did "Loch Lomond." So there it goes again on that album.
"You're Driving Me Crazy," I had been doing for quite some time. I did it when I went out to do Dick Gibson's jazz party (unintelligible) that year.
It's an up tempo number and I like it. It fits in pretty good.
And we decided to call the album "Closest Pages In A Book." And that's included in the album also.
Since that time, I've had a better chance of getting away from the folk idiom. I'm thinking that a whole lot of people are discovering that I can do something else besides "Loch Lomond."
Because I do these songs all the time, and I get requests for them, especially "Harlem Butterfly" and "Every Time, Every Time I Fall In Love."
I included "As Long As I Live" in my repertoire right after I made the album purely for identification purposes. And that I could say it's in

Yeah.
So, those two that you mentioned are
the most heavily requested of that set of songs.
Right.
